title: Estimating methods: analytical, analogous & parametric
blurb: Name the three typical estimating methods, how each works, and when each one fits.
question: At concept stage, a sponsor wants a quick cost for a new health centre. There is no work breakdown yet, but the organisation built a very similar centre two years ago. Which estimating method fits, and what is its main weakness?

teach.h: Three ways to put a number on the work
teach.body: Estimating means forecasting the time, cost and resources a project will need. The PFQ syllabus names three typical estimating methods: ANALYTICAL, ANALOGOUS and PARAMETRIC. They differ in what they are built from: the detailed work itself, a similar past project, or a proven rate from historical data. The right choice depends on how much you know at that moment and what data you hold.

teach.caption: Learn the three names as a set. Words such as budgeting, benchmarking or levelling are not estimating methods.

teach.body: Formally: each work package or activity in the work breakdown structure (WBS) is estimated in detail, and the estimates are added up to give the total. Plainly: price every piece, then add the pieces together. It is the MOST ACCURATE method because nothing is guessed at a high level, but it is TIME-CONSUMING and needs a detailed WBS, so it is only possible later, once the work has been defined.

teach.h: Analytical in action: estimates roll up

root.label: Clinic refurbishment: £84k
root.sub: the sum of the work packages

teach.caption: Each work package is estimated by the people who know that work, then rolled up. Illustrative figures only: the exam never tests arithmetic.

teach.body: Formally: the estimate is based on the actual cost or duration of a similar past project, adjusted for known differences such as size, complexity or inflation. Plainly: 'the last one cost this, ours is a bit bigger'. It is QUICK, CHEAP and usable EARLY, before any detail exists. It is LESS ACCURATE and relies on judgement and a genuinely comparable project. A 'comparative estimate' is the same thing.

Formally: a statistical relationship between historical data and a variable is used to calculate the estimate. Plainly: take a proven rate, such as cost per square metre, per metre of cable or per screen, and multiply it by how many you need. It is fast once the rate exists and can be quite accurate, but its accuracy depends entirely on the QUALITY of the data and on the relationship holding for this project.

teach.h: The three methods side by side

head: When
Method
What the estimator does
rows: Eastfield centre cost £1.2m; ours is similar, so about £1.2m–£1.5m
£2,400 per m² × 500 m² = £1.2m, as a cross-check

teach.caption: Methods can be combined: one is often used to sense-check another. Figures are illustrative.

teach.text: Don't be fooled by the names. ANALYTICAL sounds statistical but it is the bottom-up, add-up-the-pieces method. PARAMETRIC is the one using a statistical rate. ANALOGOUS means comparative (a similar past project). Budgeting is not an estimating method.

teach.body: Three-point estimating asks for an optimistic, a most likely and a pessimistic figure for an activity, to reflect uncertainty. It is a useful extra technique, but the three methods the syllabus names are analytical, analogous and parametric. Whichever method is used, record the assumptions behind the estimate so it can be checked and refined later.

items: Analytical (bottom-up): estimate each WBS work package and add them up. Most accurate, slowest, needs detail.
Analogous (comparative): scale a similar past project. Quick and early, least accurate, needs a true comparison.
Parametric: historical rate × quantity. Only as good as its data.
Early on use analogous or parametric; once the WBS exists, use analytical.

summary: You can now name the three typical estimating methods, explain how analytical, analogous and parametric estimates are produced, and weigh their strengths and weaknesses. You can choose the right method for the stage of the project and the data available.

A.q: Which estimating method builds a total by estimating each work package in the WBS and adding the estimates together?
options: Analogous
Parametric
Three-point
Analytical
A.why: Analytical (bottom-up) estimating prices each work package or activity in detail and sums them to give the total.

whyNot.0: Analogous estimating scales a similar past project; it does not price each work package.
whyNot.1: Parametric estimating multiplies a historical rate by a quantity; it does not add up work packages.
whyNot.2: Three-point estimating gives optimistic, most likely and pessimistic figures; it is not the bottom-up summing method.

A.q: An estimator takes the actual cost of a similar warehouse built two years ago and adjusts it for size and inflation. Which method is this?
options: Parametric estimating
Analogous estimating
Analytical estimating
Three-point estimating
A.why: Basing an estimate on a similar past project, adjusted for differences, is analogous (comparative) estimating.

whyNot.0: Parametric would apply a rate, such as cost per square metre, to a quantity, not copy one project's total.
whyNot.2: Analytical would estimate every work package separately and add them up.
whyNot.3: Three-point estimating uses optimistic, most likely and pessimistic values, not a comparison with one past project.

A.q: Which statement about parametric estimating is correct?
options: It relies on the judgement of a single expert
It scales a historical rate by the quantity of work
It adds up an estimate for every activity in the WBS
It copies the total cost of one earlier project
A.why: Parametric estimating uses a statistical relationship from historical data, a rate, multiplied by the quantity required.

whyNot.0: Parametric estimating is driven by data, not by one person's judgement.
whyNot.2: Summing every activity in the WBS describes analytical (bottom-up) estimating.
whyNot.3: Using one earlier project's total, adjusted, describes analogous estimating.

B.q: What is the main drawback of analytical estimating?
options: It needs a detailed WBS and takes time
It cannot be used for cost, only time
It is the least accurate of the methods
It depends on one comparable project
B.why: Analytical estimating needs the work broken down in detail, so it is time-consuming and only possible once the WBS exists.

whyNot.1: Analytical estimating works for cost, time and resources alike.
whyNot.2: It is the most accurate method, not the least.
whyNot.3: Depending on one comparable project is the weakness of analogous estimating.

B.q: A cabling contractor prices a job at £18 per metre of cable laid, a rate taken from its records of past jobs. What does the accuracy of this estimate mainly depend on?
options: How many work packages are in the WBS
How similar one past job was overall
The quality of the historical rate data
The optimism of the most likely figure
B.why: This is parametric estimating, and a parametric estimate is only as good as the historical data behind its rate.

whyNot.0: The number of work packages matters to analytical estimating, not to a rate × quantity estimate.
whyNot.1: Similarity to one past job is what matters for analogous estimating.
whyNot.3: Optimistic and most likely figures belong to three-point estimating.

B.q: Complete the statement: an analogous estimate is also known as a ____ estimate.
options: comparative
parametric
analytical
bottom-up
B.why: Analogous estimating compares the project with a similar past one, so it is also called comparative (or top-down) estimating.

whyNot.1: Parametric is a separate method based on a historical rate × quantity.
whyNot.2: Analytical is the bottom-up method, the opposite approach to analogous.
whyNot.3: Bottom-up is another name for analytical estimating, the opposite approach to analogous.

C.q:
Which TWO of the following are strengths of analogous estimating?
1) It is quick and cheap to produce
2) It is the most accurate method
3) It can be used early, before detailed plans exist
4) It needs no judgement from the estimator
options: 1 and 2
2 and 4
1 and 3
3 and 4
C.why: Analogous estimating is quick and cheap (1) and can be used early, before any WBS exists (3).

whyNot.0: Statement 2 is wrong: analytical estimating is the most accurate; analogous is the least.
whyNot.1: Both statements are wrong: analogous is not the most accurate, and it relies heavily on judgement.
whyNot.3: Statement 4 is wrong: adjusting a past project for differences needs expert judgement.

C.q: At concept stage, a sponsor asks for the cost of a new website. The organisation has built a near-identical site, but holds no per-page cost data and has no WBS yet. Which method fits best?
options: Analytical estimating
Parametric estimating
Three-point estimating
Analogous estimating
C.why: With a near-identical past project and no detail yet, analogous (comparative) estimating is the quick, early method that fits.

whyNot.0: Analytical estimating needs a detailed WBS, which does not exist yet.
whyNot.1: Parametric estimating needs reliable rate data, such as cost per page, which the organisation does not hold.
whyNot.2: Three-point estimating needs activity-level figures, which are not yet known.

C.q: A project manager now has a full WBS for a factory fit-out, and the sponsor wants the most reliable estimate before the baseline is set. What should the project manager do?
options: Scale last year's fit-out cost up by area
Estimate each work package and sum them
Apply an industry cost per square metre
Ask the sponsor to set a target figure
C.why: With a full WBS available, analytical (bottom-up) estimating gives the most accurate figure, which is what the baseline needs.

whyNot.0: Scaling last year's cost is analogous estimating: quicker, but less accurate than the bottom-up method.
whyNot.2: An industry rate is parametric estimating: useful as a check, but less precise than estimating each work package.
whyNot.3: A target set by the sponsor is not an estimate of the work at all.

reteach.title: Pricing a kitchen refit three ways
reteach.question: You want a new kitchen and need a price. How would you work it out if you asked a neighbour, a fitter's price list, or a detailed quote?

blocks.h: Three ways to price the same kitchen
blocks.body: Ask your neighbour: their kitchen was a similar size and cost £15k, so yours will be roughly the same. That is ANALOGOUS. Use a fitter's rate: about £1,000 per metre of units, and you need 14 metres. That is PARAMETRIC. Get an itemised quote: units, worktops, appliances, plumbing, electrics, tiling and labour, each priced and added up. That is ANALYTICAL.

head: Method
Kitchen version
Trade-off
rows: Instant, but their kitchen isn't yours
Fast, if the rate is reliable
blocks.caption: Illustrative figures. You would start with the neighbour's figure and finish with the itemised quote.

blocks.text: The itemised quote (analytical) can only be produced once you know exactly what you want, just as a project needs its WBS before bottom-up estimating is possible.

explain.body: Estimate every work package or activity in the WBS, then add them up. The most accurate method, but slow, and only possible once the work is broken down in detail.

explain.h: How a bottom-up estimate is built

test.q: Why is analytical estimating usually the most accurate method?
options: Each piece of work is estimated in detail
It uses an industry-wide statistical model
It is produced very early in the concept phase
It relies on the sponsor's own experience
test.why: Because every work package is estimated individually, nothing is guessed at a high level, which makes it the most accurate.

whyNot.1: A statistical model describes parametric estimating.
whyNot.2: Analytical estimating is produced later, once a WBS exists, not early at concept.
whyNot.3: It relies on detailed estimates of the work, usually from those doing it, not on the sponsor's experience.

explain.body: Take the actual cost or duration of a similar past project and adjust it for differences. Quick, cheap and usable at concept, but less accurate, and only valid if the past project really is comparable.

test.q: What does analogous estimating need above all to be reliable?
options: A fully decomposed work breakdown
A genuinely comparable past project
A large set of per-unit cost data
Detailed estimates from every team member
test.why: An analogous estimate is only as good as the similarity between this project and the past one it is based on.

whyNot.0: A full WBS is what analytical estimating needs.
whyNot.2: Per-unit cost data is what parametric estimating needs.
whyNot.3: Detailed estimates from the team feed analytical (bottom-up) estimating.

explain.body: Use a statistical relationship from historical data, such as cost per square metre or per metre of cable, and multiply it by the quantity needed. Fast once the rate exists; accuracy depends on the quality of the data.

explain.caption: Illustrative only: the PFQ exam does not test calculations.

test.q: Which of these is an example of parametric estimating?
options: Copying the cost of last year's similar event
Adding up quotes for each work package
Cost per square metre × the floor area
Asking three experts for their best guess
test.why: Applying a historical rate (cost per square metre) to a quantity (floor area) is parametric estimating.

whyNot.0: Copying a similar past event's cost is analogous estimating.
whyNot.1: Adding up work package quotes is analytical (bottom-up) estimating.
whyNot.3: Collecting expert guesses is expert judgement, not a rate × quantity model.

explain.body: Match the method to what you know. Early on, with little detail, use analogous (or parametric if good rate data exists). Once the WBS is built, use analytical for the most accurate figure. Methods can also be combined to cross-check each other.

test.q: Which statement best describes how the choice of estimating method changes through the life cycle?
options: Analytical early, analogous once detail exists
Parametric is used only at project closure
One method must be used for the whole project
Analogous early, analytical once detail exists
test.why: Analogous suits the early stages when little is known; analytical becomes possible, and preferred, once the WBS provides detail.

whyNot.0: This is the wrong way round: analytical needs detail, so it cannot come first.
whyNot.1: Parametric estimating can be used whenever reliable rate data exists, typically in planning, not only at closure.
whyNot.2: Methods are chosen to suit each stage and are often combined to cross-check.
